title: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?
shortTitle: Can a sealed class be abstract, and what is the impact on inheritance?
keyPoints: A sealed class can be `abstract` because `sealed` and `abstract` control two different things.
`sealed` controls which classes may extend it; `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly.
An abstract sealed class is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of concrete types sharing a common base.
The abstract base can have constructors that subclasses call via `super()` to enforce common invariants.
Because the subclass set is closed, abstract methods have a finite set of implementations.
This enables exhaustive switch: the compiler knows every possible concrete type.
An abstract sealed class with final record leaves is the cleanest Java encoding of an algebraic data type.

s1_definition.oneliner: A sealed class can be abstract: `abstract` stops direct instantiation while `sealed` restricts who may extend it, and both constraints apply at once.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Orthogonal modifiers** – `sealed` controls which classes may extend the type; `abstract` controls whether it can be instantiated directly.
- **Abstract sealed class** – cannot be instantiated, may declare abstract methods, and its concrete behaviour must come from its permitted subclasses.
- **Each subclass** – must be `final`, `sealed`, or `non-sealed`, exactly as with any sealed type.
- **Common base** – holds shared state, constructors, and concrete helper methods; subclasses override the abstract parts.
- **Algebraic data type** – an abstract sealed class with final record or final class leaves is the cleanest Java encoding of an ADT.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine National Bank of India defines an abstract concept of "Account" that describes what every account must do: report its balance and apply monthly processing. But you can never walk in and open a plain "Account"; you must open a specific product. At the same time, head office seals the concept so only three named products may ever be an Account. "Account" is both a blueprint you cannot instantiate directly (abstract) and a closed family with a fixed membership list (sealed).

sections.s3_flow:
```text
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  abstract sealed class Account              │
│  permits Savings, Current, Loan             │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│                                             │
│  abstract = cannot instantiate directly     │
│  sealed   = only permitted subtypes exist   │
│                                             │
│         Account (abstract + sealed)         │
│         ┌──────┬──────────┬────────┐        │
│         │      │          │        │        │
│         ▼      ▼          ▼        │        │
│     Savings  Current    Loan       │        │
│     (final)  (final)   (final)     │        │
│                                    │        │
│  Instantiation:                    │        │
│  new Account(...)  → COMPILE ERROR │        │
│  new Savings(...)  → OK            │        │
│                                    │        │
│  switch(account):                  │        │
│    case Savings → ...              │        │
│    case Current → ...              │        │
│    case Loan    → ...              │        │
│    // No default: exhaustive ✓     │        │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Yes, a sealed class can also be abstract, because the two modifiers control different things. `abstract` controls whether the class can be instantiated directly (no), and `sealed` controls which classes may extend it (only the permitted list). Since they govern different concerns, Java lets you combine them, and the abstract sealed class is the most idiomatic form.

The abstract base holds common fields, constructors, and concrete helper methods, and declares abstract methods for the parts that vary. Each permitted subclass overrides the abstract parts and calls the base constructor through `super()`. The base constructor can enforce invariants like ensuring amounts are positive, which applies to every concrete type.

The impact on inheritance is twofold. Because the base is abstract, nobody can create a plain base instance, so all instantiation is pushed to the concrete leaves. Because the base is sealed, the set of subclasses is fixed and known to the compiler, which enables exhaustive handling: a switch over the abstract sealed type covers every subclass with no `default` branch, and adding a new permitted type breaks the build until it is handled.

In a banking project at National Bank of India, Pankaj models the account base as abstract and sealed, permitting savings, current, and loan. The interest service uses an exhaustive switch to apply a regulatory cap centrally, with no default branch because the compiler knows the set is complete. The savings account earns four percent, current earns nothing, and loan charges eight-point-five percent, and each is verified exhaustively.

Remember one sentence: a sealed class can be abstract because `sealed` controls who extends it and `abstract` prevents direct instantiation, and the combination is the idiomatic way to define a closed family of concrete types.
